newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Hijacker seizes 30 hostages in south Russia.
newsitem.headline: Hijacker seizes 30 hostages in south Russia.

text.p: An man with an assault rifle and a hand grenade seized 30 hostages aboard a bus on Monday in the southern Russian region of Dagestan, officials said.

A spokesman for the regional interior ministry told Reuters by telephone that the unidentified man had been among passengers on a bus heading for the town of Kizlyar when he forced the driver to turn around and stop some 10 km (seven miles) outside Dagestan's capital, Makhachkala.

Itar-Tass news agency said the attacker was also armed with a grenade launcher and had explosives packed around his body, and that he had later freed 14 hostages -- seven women, six children and one elderly man.
But officials in Makhachkala, who are closely monitoring the crisis, could not confirm that any hostages had been freed or that the gunman had explosives.
The head of the nearby airport police was conducting negotiations with the man, who demanded a helicopter.
Tass quoted a Dagestani interior ministry official as saying he also wanted $100,000.

Officials in Dagestan, which borders Chechnya, and at the Russian Emergencies Ministry in Moscow said they had no information on who the man was, where he wanted to go or whether he might also have accomplices on board.
Tass said that the hijacker was an ethnic Abkhazian but it was not clear whether he came from the breakaway region of Georgia.

Hijackings have not been uncommon in Russia's turbulent North Caucasus. Many have involved Chechens fighting for independence for their mainly Moslem region but others have been staged for ransom or unplanned responses to police searches.

Last September a man armed with a grenade hijacked a bus in Makhachkala and demanded a helicopter. He fled by car after freeing the passengers and taking a local politician along as security, and was later reported to have crossed into Chechnya on foot.
There were two bloody hostage-takings just beyond Chechnya's borders during the conflict there from December 1994 to August 1996, one of them at Kizlyar in January 1996.

In 1994, Chechen bandits mounted a series of bus hijackings for ransom across the North Caucausus. They were cited by the Russian authorities as a reason for launching their military campaign against the secessionist rebel government in Chechnya.
